clinicalPearls: An abnormal air-filled dilatation of the laryngeal saccule that communicates with the airway, classified as internal, external, or combined depending on its relation to the thyrohyoid membrane
Internal laryngoceles bulge into the false fold and aryepiglottic fold causing hoarseness or a globus sensation, while external ones present as a reducible lateral neck swelling
Classically expands with raised intralaryngeal pressure, as in glassblowers, wind-instrument players, and chronic coughers
The lesion may enlarge on a Valsalva manoeuvre and produce a resonant swelling that empties with gentle compression
An air-filled cavity becoming fluid-filled or infected forms a laryngopyocele, which can present acutely with pain and airway threat
Imaging with CT demonstrates the air- or fluid-filled sac and defines its internal and external components
Definitive treatment is surgical excision, by an endoscopic or external cervical approach according to type and size
reference.pathophysiology: A laryngocele is an air-containing dilatation of the laryngeal saccule, the small blind-ending pouch that arises from the anterior ventricle between the true and false vocal folds. Persistently raised pressure within the larynx, or narrowing of the saccular opening, allows air to distend the saccule while maintaining its communication with the airway. If it stays medial to the thyrohyoid membrane it remains internal; if it herniates through the membrane alongside the superior laryngeal neurovascular bundle it becomes external. Because a saccular obstruction can also produce a fluid-filled saccular cyst, an important consideration is a coexisting mucosal neoplasm at the saccular opening, particularly in adults.
additionalDifferentials: Thyroglossal or other cervical cystic swelling
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy, ideally with a Valsalva manoeuvre to demonstrate expansion
CT of the neck to characterise the air- or fluid-filled sac and its components
MRI where soft-tissue detail or an underlying tumour is in question
Careful endoscopic inspection of the ventricle and saccular opening for an obstructing lesion
Histology of the excised sac and any associated mucosal lesion
redFlags: An underlying obstructing tumour at the saccular opening, especially in an older adult who does not overuse the voice
Features of a laryngopyocele with pain, fever, and rapidly enlarging swelling threatening the airway
Progressive stridor or dyspnoea from a large internal component
Rapid or unilateral enlargement without a pressure-related occupation
reference.prognosis: Surgical excision is usually curative with a low recurrence rate, and the outlook is excellent provided any underlying obstructing neoplasm is identified and treated and infective complications are avoided.
pitfalls: Assuming a laryngocele is purely idiopathic and missing an obstructing saccular tumour in an adult
Draining a laryngopyocele without addressing the underlying sac and airway risk
Underestimating the external component and planning an inadequate approach
Failing to warn wind players or glassblowers about the aggravating role of raised intralaryngeal pressure
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
